queue.label: Blood-vessels are arranged for minimum effort and minimum wall-surface
queue.text: The form and arrangement of blood-vessels are such that circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort and a minimum of wall-surface (and hence of friction).

queue.label: Shape of paired cells depends on relative tensions at outer surface and partition
queue.text: Whether two adjacent cells in a filament (as in Nostoc and its allies) are separated by flat partitions, are hemispherical, or are each more than a hemisphere depends on the relative magnitudes of the tension at the outer cell surface and at the boundary between the cells.

queue.label: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers
queue.text: Although food sets the upper limit to a species' increase, very often it is destruction by predators rather than food supply that determines the species' average numbers.

queue.label: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera
queue.text: Through natural selection and divergence of character, the small differences between varieties of a species steadily increase until they equal the larger differences between species of the same genus, or even between genera.

queue.label: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends
queue.text: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.

queue.label: Egg form obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P, the equation of all eggs
queue.text: The shape of an egg, as an extensible membrane filled with incompressible fluid under external pressure, obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P (external normal pressure plus membrane tension times total curvature equals internal pressure), which Thompson calls the equation of all eggs.

queue.label: The number of past intermediate and transitional links was inconceivably great
queue.text: Because all living species are connected through extinct parent-species back to the common ancestor of each great class by steps no greater than those between varieties, the number of intermediate and transitional forms that have lived on earth must have been inconceivably great.

queue.label: Active larvae are adapted to their own conditions as fully as adults
queue.text: Whenever an embryo or larva becomes active and must provide for itself, it is as perfectly adapted to its conditions of life as the adult, and such adaptations can make the larvae of allied species differ as much as or more than their adults, though most larvae still follow the law of embryonic resemblance.

queue.label: Computers enable discoveries beyond working out mathematical equations
queue.text: Computers are not limited to computing the consequences of mathematical equations; directly studying the behavior of even the simplest computer programs yields fundamental scientific discoveries.

queue.label: Beyond a threshold, more complex rules do not give more complex behavior
queue.text: At least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules of a system does not lead to more complex overall behavior; in cellular automata, all the ingredients for the most complex behavior already exist in the elementary two-color rules.

queue.label: Four head states suffice for random-looking Turing machine behavior
queue.text: Two-color Turing machines with four head states can produce seemingly random behavior (about five in every million such rules), and allowing more than four states makes apparent randomness only slightly more common without changing the kinds of behavior seen.

queue.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only produce nested patterns
queue.text: Substitution systems in which each element is replaced according to its own color alone always produce nested patterns, so obtaining behavior more complicated than nesting requires rules that depend on at least one neighboring element.

queue.label: Short programs in ordinary low-level languages can behave randomly
queue.text: Because register machines idealize programs in low-level languages such as C, Basic, Java or assembler, searching many millions of short programs in such languages typically yields at least a few with complex, seemingly random behavior.

queue.label: The rule-complexity threshold for complex behavior is very low
queue.text: Systems with sufficiently simple rules show only repetition, slightly more complicated rules often add nesting, and complex behavior requires crossing a threshold in rule complexity, but in every kind of system studied this threshold is extremely low.

queue.label: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences
queue.text: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.

queue.label: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all
queue.text: Most multiway systems (which keep all sequences produced by all possible replacements at each step) either grow exponentially fast or do not grow at all; slow growth is rare.

queue.label: The simplest constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern forces a nested one
queue.text: Among 2D template constraints that also require one template to appear somewhere, systematic search over more than 18 million constraints finds that the first constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern (number 18762389) forces a unique nested pattern.

queue.label: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat
queue.text: Any system of limited size made of discrete elements and following definite rules must eventually exhibit repetitive behavior, with repetition period at most equal to its total number of possible states.

queue.label: Allowed-sequence networks grow fast for class 3 and 4, slowly for 1 and 2
queue.text: As cellular automata evolve, the set of cell sequences that can occur generally becomes progressively restricted; the finite networks describing these sets stay simple (about t^2 nodes after t steps) for class 1 and 2 rules but grow at least exponentially for most class 3 and 4 rules, apart from surjective rules started from all possible sequences.

queue.label: Continuity requires slow features relative to small-scale random changes
queue.text: Continuous large-scale behavior can arise in a system with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes; for growth, the random small-scale changes must occur much faster than the overall growth.

queue.label: Continuum behavior emerges from discrete randomizing conserving rules
queue.text: Smooth continuum behavior, such as diffusion of density, emerges from discrete systems whenever small-scale apparent randomness washes out individual details and conserved quantities constrain overall features, as shown by block cellular automata whose average density follows the diffusion equation.

queue.label: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test
queue.text: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small spread of those frequencies.

queue.label: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability
queue.text: As systems of a given type are given progressively greater computational capabilities they eventually pass a threshold of universality, after which the set of computations they can perform is always the same, so more sophisticated rules gain nothing further and a universal system's capabilities are independent of the details of its construction.

queue.label: Combinators show highly complex behavior despite simple rules
queue.text: Combinators, symbolic systems long known to be universal, show highly complex behavior despite simple rules—for example a length-8 initial expression grows exponentially with seemingly random internal structure—and they can emulate rule 110, suggesting their universality is just associated with general complex behavior.

queue.label: Complicated molecules generally do not reach minimum-energy configurations
queue.text: Although simple molecules may settle into minimum-energy configurations, complicated molecules typically do not; they explore configurations by an explicit evolution process, so nature does not actually solve hard constraint-satisfaction problems as traditional models idealize.

queue.label: Exhaustive search of 2-state 2-color Turing machines finds three growth rates
queue.text: Enumerating all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors shows that the maximum number of steps to finish a computation grows with input length only linearly, quadratically, or exponentially, and every exponential case has another such machine computing the same function in bounded steps.

queue.label: Diverse computational systems emulate each other with comparable step counts
queue.text: Almost all the varied systems considered (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution and other systems) can emulate each other in a comparable number of steps, typically with at most polynomial overhead such as t^2 or t^(d+1), so rates of computation do not differ greatly across systems, including presumably those in nature.

queue.label: P is likely different from NP
queue.text: It is likely that in most meaningful senses there is no general way to determine whether any path of a multiway or non-deterministic system yields a given outcome in a number of steps growing only polynomially, i.e. P is not equal to NP.

queue.label: Gödel's Theorem follows from the universality of arithmetic, shown via rule 110
queue.text: An integer (exponential Diophantine) equation can be built whose solutions emulate the rule 110 cellular automaton; since rule 110 is universal, the axioms of arithmetic support universality, which implies Gödel's Theorem that arithmetic contains statements that cannot be proved true or false. Wolfram presents Gödel's Theorem as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.

queue.label: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens
queue.text: The human curve of growth in stature shows rapid increase in infancy, a long period of slower, nearly steady growth in early boyhood, a marked quickening in the early teens, and finally a gradual arrest as full height is reached.

queue.label: Boys and girls share a growth-velocity curve differing mainly in phase
queue.text: The curves of growth velocity in boys and girls are of very similar shape but differ in amplitude and especially in phase, the girl's adolescent acceleration beginning and ending earlier than the boy's.

queue.label: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate
queue.text: Hard-shelled eggs, while often pointed, are never flattened or discoidal: they are prolate, never oblate, solids of revolution.

queue.label: Frogs, toads and newts are absent from oceanic islands
queue.text: Batrachians (frogs, toads and newts) are naturally absent from oceanic islands, not because conditions there are unsuitable (introduced frogs thrive) but because they and their spawn are killed by sea-water and so cannot cross the sea.

queue.label: Fresh-water fish species are not shared between distant continents
queue.text: The same species of fresh-water fish never occur in the fresh waters of distant continents, although within a continent fish species often range widely and irregularly, different river systems sharing some species but not others.

queue.label: Northern species naturalise far more often in the south than the reverse
queue.text: At the present day many European species have become naturalised and partly displaced the natives in La Plata and to a lesser degree in Australia, whereas extremely few southern-hemisphere species have become naturalised anywhere in Europe.

queue.label: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species
queue.text: Although terrestrial mammals are absent from oceanic islands, bats occur on almost every island, and remote islands often have their own endemic bat species, because bats can fly across wide spaces of sea and are then modified in their new homes.

queue.label: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
queue.text: Blind cave animals of America should be most closely allied to other inhabitants of America, and those of Europe to inhabitants of Europe, rather than the cave faunas of the two continents being specially similar to each other.

queue.label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
queue.text: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.

queue.label: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas
queue.text: Neither the similarity nor the dissimilarity of the inhabitants of different regions can be explained by their climate and other physical conditions; regions with closely parallel conditions (e.g. Australia, South Africa and western South America at 25°–35° S) have utterly different faunas and floras.

queue.label: Fossils from consecutive formations are more alike than those from remote ones
queue.text: Fossils from two consecutive formations are far more closely related to each other than fossils from two formations widely separated in time, and the fauna of each period is broadly intermediate between those before and after it.
